articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than culverts. Records show why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 3 of 47 priority drainage projects
Public records show $8.1 million spent on engineering studies and consultants, while $31 million sits unspent in reserve accounts
County staff blame permitting delays and contractor shortages, but internal emails reveal deeper dysfunction in project management
articles.body:
The drainage ditch behind Carla Hutchins' house on Doris Drive floods every time it rains more than an inch. She knows this because she started keeping a log in 2019. The notebook sits on her kitchen counter, 47 entries deep.

"They told me the stormwater fee would fix this," Hutchins said, standing in her backyard where brown water pooled around her azaleas after last week's afternoon storm. "I've paid $720 into that fund. Where did it go?"

Three years after Escambia County voters approved a dedicated stormwater utility fee—sold as the solution to chronic flooding that damages hundreds of homes annually—the county has collected $47.2 million and completed exactly three projects from its original priority list of 47.

The Flightline obtained 1,400 pages of internal documents, contracts and financial records through public records requests spanning eight months. They reveal a program paralyzed by consultant dependency, bureaucratic infighting and what one county engineer called "analysis paralysis" in an email to colleagues.

The Money Trail

When voters approved the stormwater fee in November 2022, county officials promised a systematic approach to drainage problems that had plagued neighborhoods for decades. The fee—$7.50 per month for single-family homes, scaled rates for commercial properties—would generate roughly $16 million annually.

The 2023 budget projected eight completed projects by end of year. The 2024 budget projected 15 more. Reality delivered far less.

According to financial records through May 2026:

  • Total collected: $47.2 million
  • Spent on construction: $6.3 million (three projects)
  • Spent on consultants and engineering studies: $8.1 million
  • Administrative overhead: $1.8 million
  • Held in reserve: $31 million

The three completed projects—drainage improvements on Navy Boulevard, a retention pond expansion near Ensley and culvert replacements on Mobile Highway—were already in the design phase before the fee passed. New projects initiated since 2023 remain stuck in various stages of study and permitting.

Consultants Studying Consultants

The largest single expenditure has been a $3.2 million master planning contract awarded to CDM Smith, a national engineering firm, in March 2023. The contract was amended twice, adding $900,000 for "additional watershed analysis" and "stakeholder engagement services."

CDM Smith delivered a 340-page master plan in December 2024. The county then hired a second firm, Kimley-Horn, for $1.1 million to review the master plan and develop implementation priorities.

"We needed an independent set of eyes," Public Works Director Marcus Bellamy said in a May interview. "These are complex hydrological systems. You don't just start digging ditches."

But internal emails tell a different story. In September 2024, Senior Engineer Patricia Womack wrote to colleagues: "We are paying KH to tell us what CDM already told us. This is CYA, not engineering."

Womack declined to comment for this article. Bellamy said the email was "taken out of context" and reflected "healthy internal debate."

Permitting Purgatory

Four projects did advance to design phase in 2024. All four remain stalled.

The Scenic Highway drainage project, estimated at $4.7 million, has been awaiting Florida Department of Environmental Protection permits for 14 months. A wetlands mitigation plan required by the permit was submitted in March 2025 and rejected twice for technical deficiencies.

The Brent Lane retention pond, budgeted at $2.1 million, requires a land swap with the Escambia County School District that has been in negotiation since January 2025. School district officials say the county's initial offer undervalued the parcel by $300,000.

"Every project hits three or four walls," said Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who supported the original fee referendum. "It's not one thing. It's permitting, land acquisition, contractor availability, FEMA coordination. We underestimated the friction."

Commissioner Lumon May offered a blunter assessment at the June 18 board meeting: "We told voters we knew what we were doing. Clearly we did not."

The Contractor Problem

Even projects that clear permitting face another obstacle: contractors who won't bid on them.

The county issued requests for proposals on seven drainage projects in 2025. Three received zero bids. Two received single bids at 40% above engineer estimates. Only two attracted competitive bidding.

Bellamy blamed market conditions. Hurricane recovery work across the Gulf Coast has absorbed regional construction capacity. Wages for heavy equipment operators have risen 35% since 2022.

"Contractors can make more money doing private work or FEMA-funded projects in Louisiana," Bellamy said. "We're competing for a limited labor pool."

The county has not adjusted its fee structure to account for inflated construction costs. The original project list, developed in 2022, assumed costs that have since risen an average of 28% according to industry indices.

Neighborhoods Still Waiting

The Brownsville neighborhood in central Pensacola appears on the priority list at number seven. Residents there collected 340 signatures on a petition delivered to commissioners in April, documenting 22 homes that flooded during Hurricane Sally in 2020 and again during unnamed storms in 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Lillian Waters has lived on Haynes Street for 31 years. She voted for the stormwater fee. She attended three public meetings. She filed 14 service requests with the county.

"They sent somebody out to look at the ditch," Waters said. "He took pictures and left. That was February last year. Nothing since."

County records show the Brownsville project is in "watershed assessment phase." No design contract has been issued. No construction timeline exists.

"We prioritize based on severity and feasibility," Bellamy said. "Some neighborhoods have problems that require regional solutions. You can't fix one block without addressing the whole system."

Waters found this explanation inadequate. "They always have a reason," she said. "Meanwhile my carpet's ruined again."

What Comes Next

The Board of County Commissioners will receive an updated stormwater program report at its July 17 meeting. Staff recommendations include raising the monthly fee to $9.50 to account for cost inflation and hiring three additional project managers to accelerate permitting work.

Commissioners May and Bergosh have both expressed skepticism about fee increases before demonstrating progress. Commissioner Steven Barry suggested at a June work session that the county consider outsourcing project management entirely to a private firm.

"We've proven we can't do this ourselves," Barry said. "Maybe it's time to admit that."

The $31 million in reserves continues to accrue interest—approximately $1.4 million in 2025 according to county finance records. That money cannot be spent on anything except stormwater infrastructure without voter approval to dissolve the utility.

On Doris Drive, Carla Hutchins is not optimistic. She has started pricing out a private drainage solution for her backyard. Estimates range from $8,000 to $15,000.

"I'll probably just do it myself," she said. "At least then I'll know where the money went."

The Flightline requested interviews with all five county commissioners, Public Works Director Marcus Bellamy and CDM Smith project managers. Bellamy and Commissioner Bergosh agreed to interviews. Commissioner May provided a written statement. Commissioners Barry, Doug Underhill and Chair Robert Bender did not respond to requests. CDM Smith declined to comment, citing client confidentiality.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Last Fish House on Perdido Key
articles.dek: Flora-Bama's neighbor has sold bait and ice for 61 years. A Virginia developer wants the land for 200 condos. The owner isn't ready to talk price.
brief: Ole River Fish House has operated on Perdido Key since 1965, making it the last bait-and-tackle shop on the barrier island
Tidewater Capital Partners has approached owner Earl Sutton multiple times about purchasing the 2.3-acre property for a planned 200-unit condominium development
Sutton, 79, says he's not interested in selling but acknowledges his children may face a different calculation
articles.body:
The cooler by the front door holds exactly what it has held since Lyndon Johnson was president: dead shrimp on ice, blood worms in newspaper, and a hand-lettered sign that says CASH ONLY.

Earl Sutton refills it every morning at 4:30. He has done this approximately 22,000 times.

"I don't count," he said, standing behind the register at Ole River Fish House on a Tuesday morning in late June. "Counting makes you tired."

Outside, past the shell-and-gravel parking lot and the gas pumps that still sell non-ethanol marine fuel, the Ole River meets Perdido Bay in a tangle of oyster beds and sea grass. A great blue heron stood motionless on a piling. Three pickup trucks with empty boat trailers waited in the shade.

This is what 2.3 acres of unreconstructed Florida looks like in 2026. It looks like money.

The Offer

Tidewater Capital Partners, a Norfolk-based real estate investment firm, has approached Sutton four times since January about purchasing Ole River Fish House and the surrounding property. The company's most recent letter, dated May 15 and reviewed by The Flightline, did not specify a dollar amount but invited Sutton to "begin a conversation about the future of this exceptional waterfront parcel."

The letter referenced Tidewater's plans for a 200-unit condominium development with "resort-style amenities" and "direct bay access." It noted the company's successful completion of similar projects in Virginia Beach, Destin and Panama City Beach.

Sutton keeps the letters in a folder behind the register, next to the tide charts and the list of customers who owe him money for gas.

"They're polite," he said. "I'll give them that."

He has not responded to any of them.

Tidewater Capital Partners did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

61 Years of Bait

Earl Sutton's father, Vernon Sutton, bought the property in 1962 for $8,500. He built the fish house three years later with concrete blocks, cypress beams and a tin roof that has been replaced exactly once, after Hurricane Ivan in 2004.

Vernon Sutton died in 1989. Earl took over. His wife, Darlene, handled the books until her death in 2019. Now Earl does everything.

The business model has not changed in six decades. Bait, ice, gas, cold drinks, fishing tackle, boat launch access for $10. No credit cards. No website. No social media presence.

"People find us," Sutton said.

They do. On the morning of The Flightline's visit, a steady stream of customers came through: a father and son from Mobile buying shrimp for a speckled trout trip, a retired couple from Pensacola picking up ice for their cooler, a commercial crabber named Dale who has been buying fuel here since 1978.

"Only place left that sells non-ethanol," Dale said, filling two five-gallon cans. "Everything else out here is condos and T-shirt shops."

The Geography of Change

He is not wrong. The Perdido Key that Vernon Sutton knew in 1965 no longer exists.

That year, the barrier island's population was roughly 200 permanent residents, according to historical census estimates. The Flora-Bama Lounge, now a sprawling entertainment complex that straddles the Florida-Alabama line, was a small bar with a dirt parking lot.

Today, Perdido Key's permanent population exceeds 3,500, with a seasonal population that can triple that figure. The corridor along Perdido Key Drive is dominated by condominium towers—Palacio, Beach Colony, Vista del Mar—that range from 15 to 22 stories.

According to Escambia County property records, the median assessed value of waterfront property on Perdido Key increased 340% between 2000 and 2025. Ole River Fish House sits on one of the last undeveloped waterfront parcels on the Florida side of the key.

The Escambia County Property Appraiser's office lists the current assessed value of the Sutton property at $2.1 million. Real estate professionals who spoke with The Flightline estimated the market value for development purposes at between $8 million and $12 million.

"That's a conservative estimate," said Marcus Webb, a commercial real estate broker with Pensacola-based Coastal Realty Partners. Webb is not involved in any negotiations regarding the property. "Waterfront with bay access, that close to Flora-Bama? You could make an argument for higher."

The Question of What Comes Next

Earl Sutton has three children. His son, Earl Jr., works for the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission in Tallahassee. His daughters, Beth and Christine, live in Birmingham and Atlanta, respectively. None of them have expressed interest in running the fish house.

"They have their own lives," Sutton said. "I don't blame them."

He is 79 years old. His knees hurt. The 4:30 mornings are harder than they used to be.

Asked directly whether he intends to sell, Sutton was quiet for a long moment. Behind him, the ancient cash register sat open, showing a thin stack of fives and ones.

"Not today," he said finally. "Ask me again tomorrow."

He reached under the counter and pulled out a plastic bucket of frozen cigar minnows. A customer had just pulled up, a young woman in a Pensacola State College T-shirt with a kayak strapped to the roof of her car.

"What are you after?" Sutton asked her.

"Redfish," she said. "Maybe flounder."

"Minnows and shrimp," he said. "Work the grass flats on the outgoing tide."

He rang her up. Eight dollars and fifty cents. She paid with a ten and told him to keep the change.

The screen door banged shut behind her. Sutton watched her drive toward the boat ramp, then turned back to the cooler by the front door. The ice was melting. It always is.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels 2027 Season in Doubt After Navy Cuts Training Budget
articles.dek: Internal documents show Pensacola's signature attraction faces its first canceled season since the 2013 sequester. NAS Pensacola officials won't comment.
brief: Internal Navy budget documents obtained by The Flightline show the Blue Angels demonstration squadron faces a 62% reduction in flight demonstration funding for fiscal year 2027.
The cuts would force cancellation of all 2027 air shows—the first full season shutdown since sequestration grounded the team in 2013.
NAS Pensacola's public affairs office declined to comment, citing 'ongoing budget deliberations' within the Department of the Navy.
articles.body:
The six F/A-18 Super Hornets sat in a perfect diagonal line on the tarmac at Forrest Sherman Field last Thursday morning, their blue and gold paint catching the early sun. A maintenance crew worked beneath the lead jet. On the flight line, nothing suggested this could be the squadron's final full season.

But 400 miles away in Washington, budget documents tell a different story.

Internal Navy planning documents obtained by The Flightline show the Blue Angels Flight Demonstration Squadron faces a 62% reduction in its operational budget for fiscal year 2027. The cuts, part of a broader Navy realignment toward unmanned systems and Pacific theater readiness, would eliminate funding for all public air show appearances next year.

If the proposed budget survives congressional review, 2027 would mark the first canceled Blue Angels season since sequestration grounded the team from April through December 2013.

'Ongoing budget deliberations'

Jason Bortz, public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Pensacola, declined to confirm or deny the budget figures.

"We're aware of various planning documents circulating regarding fiscal year 2027 appropriations," Bortz said in an emailed statement. "It would be inappropriate to comment on ongoing budget deliberations within the Department of the Navy."

Bortz referred additional questions to the Chief of Naval Operations' office in Washington, which did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

The budget documents, marked "Pre-Decisional" and dated June 12, 2026, outline a reduction in Blue Angels flight demonstration funding from $38.2 million to $14.5 million. The remaining funds would cover aircraft maintenance, personnel costs and limited training flights—but no public performances.

A separate line item shows the Naval Flight Demonstration Squadron's travel and logistics budget zeroed out entirely.

Economic ripple effects

The Blue Angels perform at roughly 30 air shows annually across the United States and Canada. But the squadron's home base remains Pensacola, where twice-weekly practice sessions from March through November draw thousands of spectators to the National Naval Aviation Museum grounds.

Those practice sessions are free. The economic impact is not.

Visit Pensacola estimates Blue Angels-related tourism generates between $85 million and $120 million annually for Escambia County. That figure includes the Pensacola Beach Air Show each July, which drew an estimated 150,000 spectators in 2025.

"The Blue Angels are Pensacola," said Darien Schaefer, president of Visit Pensacola. "For a lot of families, watching practice is the reason they come here instead of Panama City or Destin. You can't replicate that anywhere else."

Schaefer said his office had not received any official notification about potential 2027 cancellations. He learned of the budget documents from a Flightline reporter.

"This is the first I'm hearing specific numbers," he said. "Obviously this would be devastating if it happens."

A familiar pattern

Budget pressure on military demonstration teams is not new. The Air Force Thunderbirds and Army Golden Knights parachute team faced similar cuts during the 2013 sequester. All three teams were grounded for roughly eight months that year.

The 2013 shutdown cost Pensacola an estimated $21 million in lost tourism revenue, according to a University of West Florida economic analysis. Hotel occupancy rates along Pensacola Beach dropped 18% during what would have been the practice season.

But 2013's cuts came suddenly, with little warning. This time, if the budget documents prove accurate, local officials would have nearly a year to prepare.

"A year doesn't help you," said Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh. "You can't market around the Blue Angels not being here. People either come to see them or they don't."

Bergosh said he planned to contact the offices of Senator Rick Scott and Representative Matt Gaetz to request intervention in the budget process.

"This needs to be a priority," Bergosh said. "I don't care what else is going on in Washington."

What happens to the pilots

The Blue Angels typically carry 17 officers, including six demonstration pilots and the commanding officer. All are active-duty Navy or Marine Corps aviators on two or three-year assignments.

The budget documents suggest the squadron would not be dissolved—only its public mission suspended. Pilots would continue training flights at NAS Pensacola while the team maintains readiness for a potential 2028 return.

"That's how it worked in 2013," said Brad Rich, a retired Navy commander who served as Blue Angels operations officer from 2008 to 2010. "The team didn't go anywhere. They just couldn't fly for crowds."

Rich, who now lives in Gulf Breeze, said a one-year hiatus would be painful but survivable. A longer suspension would create problems.

"You lose continuity," Rich said. "The guys who were supposed to train together don't. When you come back, you're essentially starting over with timing and coordination."

The 2013 grounding lasted eight months. The team required six additional weeks of practice flights before resuming public demonstrations.

What comes next

The proposed Navy budget must still clear the House and Senate Armed Services Committees before becoming final. Historically, Congress has restored funding to popular programs cut in executive budget requests—including military demonstration teams.

Representative Matt Gaetz, whose district includes NAS Pensacola, has previously championed Blue Angels funding. His office did not respond to requests for comment on the FY2027 proposal.

The Navy's final budget request goes to Congress in February 2027. Appropriations votes typically follow in late spring.

For now, the 2026 season continues as scheduled. The Blue Angels' next Pensacola practice flight is Tuesday at 11:30 a.m. The Pensacola Beach Air Show runs July 10-11.

On the tarmac at Forrest Sherman Field, the jets still gleam in their blue and gold. What happens next depends on budget votes that won't come for another year.
